analysis.one_liner: Caps consumer loan interest rates and fees at the maximum allowed by the borrower's home state.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee from April 2022 until the Congress ended in January 2023, with support from 5 of 100 senators.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Truth in Lending Act so that the interest rate and fees on any consumer loan other than a home mortgage could not exceed the maximum rate allowed in the state where the borrower lives. Today, banks can 'export' the interest rate cap of the state where the bank is chartered to borrowers in any state, which is how many online and payday-style lenders offer triple-digit annual rates in states that cap them. The bill would close that loophole by making the borrower's home state cap apply to every consumer lender.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in states with strict interest rate caps, especially low-income people who take out payday, auto-title, and installment loans currently priced above their state's cap through bank partnerships. State regulators and attorneys general enforcing consumer protection laws would also gain a clear federal rule backing their rate limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers in states with rate caps

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate, including fees, on every consumer credit transaction except home mortgages at the maximum rate allowed by the state where the consumer lives.

The cap applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' meaning it overrides the current legal structure that lets nationally chartered banks export their home state's rate cap to borrowers nationwide.

By closing the bank rate-export loophole, the bill would bring online and bank-partner lenders back under the rate limits state voters and legislatures have set, in states that cap rates as low as 36% or lower.

analysis.who_pays: High-cost consumer lenders, including payday, auto-title, and online installment lenders, and the banks and financial technology companies that partner with them to export rates, would lose the ability to charge rates above state caps. Some borrowers with poor credit might find fewer legal loan options in states with very low caps, because lenders that cannot price for their risk may stop lending there.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-cost lenders and their bank partners

drawbacks.text: The bill ties all consumer lending to the borrower's state rate cap, and in states with very low caps, lenders that cannot profitably make small loans to higher-risk borrowers may simply stop offering them, leaving those borrowers with fewer legal options and potentially pushing some to unregulated lenders.

The bill covers nearly all consumer credit except mortgages, so even mainstream products like credit cards would have to comply with each state's cap, a major operational change for national lenders who argue that standardized national pricing keeps credit available across state lines.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people in states with strict rate caps, the benefit is concrete: loans currently priced at triple-digit annual rates above the cap would be off the table, and fees could no longer be used to dodge the cap since fees count toward it. The honest cost falls on a subset of borrowers, those with the weakest credit, who might see fewer small-dollar loan options in low-cap states, though the loans they lose access to are the most expensive ones. The tradeoff is a familiar one in rate-cap policy, and the bill takes the side of capping.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died at the end of the Congress in January 2023 without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 7, 2022, joined by four cosponsors: Senators Reed, Warren, and Merkley, all Democrats, and Senator Sanders, an Independent.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No further action was ever recorded: the committee held no markup or vote, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost consumer lenders and the banks and financial technology companies that partner with them are better off, because they can continue charging rates above many states' caps through the bank rate-export structure the bill would have closed. No one who supported the bill got a vote on it.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer loan rates at the borrower's home state maximum.

for.name: Sens. Jack Reed, Elizabeth Warren, Jeff Merkley, and Bernie Sanders
for.role: Original cosponsors (3 Senate Democrats, 1 Senate Independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no other senators joined.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 7, 2022 and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the bill's five sponsors were all Democrats or the Independent Sanders, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.industry: Payday, auto-title, and high-cost installment lenders
industries.note: These lenders' business model depends on charging annual rates of several hundred percent, usually far above what most states allow. The bill would make the borrower's home state cap apply to them, eliminating their ability to lend above state limits.

industries.industry: National banks and fintech lending partnerships
industries.note: Many online lenders currently make loans through or with national banks, which can export their charter state's (often no) rate cap to borrowers in every state. The bill overrides that structure, forcing the borrower's home state cap to apply and cutting off the most profitable segment of small-dollar lending.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and mainstream consumer lenders
industries.note: The cap covers consumer credit generally, so card issuers would face state caps where they exist, though rates in most states do not tightly constrain today's typical card APRs. The effect on ordinary cardholders is small compared with the effect on small-dollar borrowers.
